message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did the right thing or not in this situation. Let me start by understanding what happened. A few years ago, I was renting a place with this dude. We were on a lease, which means we had a contract to stay there for a certain period. When the lease was almost up, he just left without giving much notice. He took most of his stuff, but left a few things and a note saying he didn't want to bring those things with him. Now, where I live, if you don't get rid of your stuff when you move out, the landlord can pay someone to remove it, and they can take money from your deposit for that. I've heard of people losing $250 just because someone had to take three milk crates of their stuff to the dump. That's a rip-off. So, I tried to contact him for two weeks, texting and emailing, asking him to pick up his stuff or let me take them to the dump. But he never responded. I ended up taking most of his stuff to the dump, but he had around 60 video games for the PS4. I thought, "Why not sell them?" There's a local game store that buys used games, and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Fast forward to last week, I was at a party where he was also there. We were being polite, but then he asked how the move-out process went. I told him it was good, and naturally, he asked what I did with his stuff. When he found out I sold his games, he got mad. I told him I tried to get him to grab those things, but he never reached out. Now he's calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked, and legally, there's nothing wrong with what I did. But now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this. Okay, so to figure this out, I need to think about the different aspects of the situation: the lease agreement, the responsibilities of both parties, the communication that happened, the financial implications, and the emotional response from the former roommate. First, the lease agreement. We were both on a lease, which means we had certain obligations. Typically, a lease outlines the responsibilities of both the landlord and the tenants, including how to handle the end of the lease term. If the lease specifies that tenants must remove their belongings by a certain date, then it's the tenant's responsibility to do so. If they don't, the landlord can take action, which in this case includes removing the belongings and charging the tenant for the cost. In this situation, the former roommate left without giving proper notice and left some of his belongings. The landlord's policy seems to be that if tenants don't remove their stuff, the landlord will have it removed and charge the tenant for it. This is a common practice to prevent the landlord from being stuck with tenants' belongings. Next, the communication aspect. I tried to contact him for two weeks, asking him to pick up his stuff or let me take them to the dump. But he never responded. This is important because it shows that I made an effort to communicate and give him a chance to handle his belongings. If he didn't respond, it's reasonable to assume that he didn't care about his stuff or didn't want to deal with it. Then, the action of selling the games. I took most of his stuff to the dump, but I kept the video games and sold them for $600. This seems like a practical solution to avoid the landlord charging me for the removal of his stuff. By selling the games, I not only prevented the landlord from charging me but also made some money from it. However, the emotional response from the former roommate is significant. He got mad when he found out I sold his games and is now calling me an asshole and asking for reimbursement. This indicates that he feels wronged, even though legally, I didn't do anything wrong. So, is selling his games without his explicit consent the right thing to do? Legally, it seems fine because I tried to contact him, and he didn't respond. But morally, is it right to sell someone's belongings without their permission, even if they abandoned them? I think it's important to consider the intent behind the action. I sold the games to prevent the landlord from charging me for their removal, which is a practical and responsible decision. However, by selling them, I also gained financially from his belongings, which might be seen as taking advantage of the situation. Another angle is the concept of abandonment. If someone leaves their belongings behind and doesn't respond to attempts to contact them, it can be interpreted as abandonment. In such cases, the landlord or other tenants might have the right to dispose of the belongings as they see fit, especially if it's causing a problem or costing money. But in this case, I went beyond just disposing of the belongings; I sold them for money. This might be where the line is drawn. While disposing of the stuff to prevent costs is one thing, profiting from it could be seen as wrong, even if legally permissible. Additionally, the emotional impact on the former roommate is significant. He felt betrayed and angry when he found out about the sale. This indicates that there's a personal value attached to those games that I didn't consider. Maybe they were sentimental, or he intended to keep them for future use. By selling them, I took away something that had value to him, even if it was just financial. So, in conclusion, while legally I didn't do anything wrong, morally, there's a gray area. Selling the games without his explicit consent, even if he abandoned them, could be seen as taking advantage of the situation. It's important to balance practicality with empathy and respect for others' belongings, even if they've been abandoned. Therefore, I think I might have crossed a line by selling his games without his permission, even though legally it was acceptable. It's essential to consider the emotional and personal implications of our actions, especially when dealing with others' belongings and relationships.
